description_full: Lattice Semiconductor Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, develops and sells semiconductor, silicon-based and silicon-enabling, evaluation boards, and development hardware products in Asia, Europe, and the Americas. It offers field programmable gate arrays (FPGA), which are regular arrays of logic that can be custom-configured by the user through software. The company's products include small FPGA platforms, including Lattice Nexus and Lattice Nexus 2; Lattice Avant, a mid-range FPGA platform; general purpose FPGA, such as Lattice Avant-G, Certus-NX, CertusPro, and Certus-N2; and specialized FPGAs, which includes Lattice Avant-E, Avant-X, SCP, MachXO, iCE, CrossLink,and CrossLinkPlus. It also provides design software that includes Lattice Radiant to deliver tools that enable predictable design convergence; Lattice Propel for creating embedded processor-based designs; develops Lattice Automate for industrial automation and robotics; Lattice mVision forlow power embedded vision; Lattice ORAN for control data security, fronthaul synchronization, and low power hardware acceleration; Lattice sensAI for Edge AI applications; Lattice Sentry for hardware security implementation; and Lattice Drive for automotive system designs and applications. In addition, the company offers Glance, an edge AI application software that allows users to control the AI and computer vision experiences for various edge applications, including client computing, industrial, and automotive applications; and sells video connectivity application specific standard products. Further, it provides standard IP and IP core licensing, patent monetization, and IP services. The company serves communications and computing, industrial and automotive, and consumer markets. Lattice Semiconductor Corporation was incorporated in 1983 and is headquartered in Hillsboro, Oregon.

financial_summary: Lattice Semiconductor Corporati is a large-cap technology business with a $14.9B market cap on $523M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 24% against a 12% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 67% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $133M in free cash flow — roughly 25 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 56.78× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -19.5% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 43× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.6%, a thin return of capital, and stock-based comp at 22% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.09x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-37.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 115% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 24% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 33% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 63% and a beta of 1.50, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.77 vs 5y 1.84), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $181.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash, 43% in the 2022 bear market and 72% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $6.31 (margin of safety -1565%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $4.68 to $8.91 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 338.8 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 93.0 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 112.7 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 1042% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $156 on average, 49% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 24% clears the cost of capital of 12.2% by 12pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.39).
It runs a 67% gross margin and converts 25% of revenue into free cash flow, or 3% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-19.5% of assets).
ROE of 0% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 35.9% of revenue on R&D and 22.1% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 54.3, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 143 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
Goodwill makes up 36% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.5% over 3 years and 5.1% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 64% of profits supports about 15.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs 2.1x depreciation (8.1% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 10 sales over the past year, net $2.0M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.6% (0.6% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 0.8% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 1,174 employees, each generates about $446K of revenue, 1.2x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 3.6% a year.
That works out to $113K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.7M (4x revenue per employee).
